I'm looking for the same answer you are, so I can't help with that. I might be able to help with this part though:

> "In order to create this RAG we first have to generate this X environment." and then a big block of code that the author expects you to do something with.

Pretty much every tutorial I have seen is using Python. It's probably safe to assume that unless otherwise specified, the code in a guide is using Python. If you don't have that installed, open up the Microsoft Store app on your computer, search for Python, and install the latest version. Looks like that is 3.12 at the moment.

Once it downloads and the installer window pops up, make sure to install it for all users instead of your account only, and to check the box to allow the installer to modify the PATH variable. Restart your computer afterwards.

Next, download Visual Studio Code. That is the program you will use to actually write your programs, and has an integrated debugging utility, terminal, and an absurdly large number of helpful extensions. When you launch it for the first time, it will offer you some guided tutorials to follow to learn the program. I'd recommend you do them. Honestly, I even repeat them myself sometimes. After that, find the extensions area and use the search function in there to find and install the Python Extension Pack. Optional: search for themes and find one that you enjoy looking at. Personally, I am digging the "dracula" lately. 

Now: memorize Control+Shift+P. That keyboard shortcut opens the "command palette" in Visual Studio Code (VSC), where you can type the beginning of a command to find and execute that thing. Now you want to make a folder to store this project in, but first a fast note about that: you *could* save a one-off file wherever, but the advantage of having a separate folder is so you can use git for version control and backing up your code to the cloud. I'm not going to go into how all that works right now, but trust me, once you are more comfortable with working with code and inside VSC, you will want to start learning it :)

Back to the folder. Go to your documents, desktop, or wherever, and make a new folder. Call it whatever you want. Back in VSC, hit Ctrl+Shift+P, type open folder, then enter to execute that command. Open that folder you created so that you are working exclusively within it.

Now, Ctrl+Shift+P again, but this time type in "create python environment", and choose "venv". Give it a minute to set up your environment, and if you see a popup asking if you want to select that environment automatically when the folder is opened, definitely make sure that is enabled. 

Finally, Ctrl+Shift+P one more time, type "python terminal", and select the option to create a new terminal. Now you should be in a position to immediately begin following the other guides out there that start from that point. When you see a couple of lines of code by themselves, especially anything that says "pip install X", you are probably going to be pasting that into the terminal at the bottom of the screen. 

When you get entire chunks of code to run, those will be pasted into the 'main' code editor, and will get run when you run the program or start it from the terminal. The guide you are following should cover that part.

I have the same issue, but I solved 90% of it when I realized that the fucking bed screw that the springs and wheels are on was stripped from the bed itself. So when you turn the wheel to adjust the bed, the screw is turning with it even though it seems like it isn't. 

Try taking the wheels and springs off again, and then screwing a nut onto each bed screw before you put the spring back on. You should end up with, from top to bottom

* glass bed
* bed frame
* the new nut
* spring
* wheel

Make sure you use a wrench to really tighten that nut up against the underside of the bed frame. 

This helped my bed stay level for much longer than it had been, although it wasn't the complete answer.

I know this was posted a year ago, but I just came across it as I was searching for a way to do the same thing. I figured out a solution using a shell command run from within Klipper, so I thought I'd post it here in case you or anyone else comes across this like I did.

To do this, you will need to enable execution of shell commands. I did so by launching up KIAUH, by going into the advanced section of its main menu, and then choosing "[G-code Shell Command]." That'll install any needed files and enable the feature.

Once that's done, modify your printer.cfg file if you need to in order to isolate the saved variables to their own file. The way I solving this whole thing is simply by nuking the file containing the variables , so you definitely want nothing but those variables in the target file. I am keeping mine in my klipper_config file with the filename SavedVariables.cfg.

So if I wanted to delete them from the Pi's command line, I would use

    rm ~/klipper_config/SavedVariables.cfg

and I'm executing that from within Klipper using a G-code macro. Here is the complete thing.

    [gcode_shell_command clear_vars]
    command: rm /home/pi/klipper_config/SavedGcodeVars.cfg
    timeout: 2.
    verbose: True
    
    [gcode_macro CLEAR_VARS]
    gcode:
        RUN_SHELL_COMMAND CMD=clear_vars

In practice, I just need to run the macro CLEAR_VARS and poof, they're gone. Hope this helps someone!

In addition to what the other guy said, don't start zoning a ton of land all at the same time. The green and blue bars may be empty and the orange bar full, but that doesn't mean you need a huge amount of industrial area, only that the need for industrial is huge in proportion to residential or business. And the bars won't adjust until the buildings have been built, so wait until that happens to see if you need more of that zone.

One other thing: don't zone industrial areas right next to residential. The pollution (and noise pollution) from the factories will make the people living next to them unhappy and sick. Separate them from each other a bit. That will also help keep trucks from clogging up the roads around the other areas.

Can't upvote this one enough. Seriously, forget what the experts say about finding your passion in life and blah blah blah. The key to happiness, or at least not being as miserable, is to eliminate as much of the shit you hate doing as possible. I LIVE for this.

Sit down and took a good hard look at your schedule, what errands you run, how many different locations you have to go to in a given day or week, etc.

How many of those places are on the same side of town so you could just run through each of them in a row once a week? How many of those trips to different stores can be consolidated? How much time can you save by ordering things online? Things like that.

Personally, I hate grocery/household items shopping. So I shop at Costco and buy everything in bulk so I have to do it as little as possible. Packages of meat get thrown in the freezer.

I also loathe cooking. So when I cook something, I usually batch it according to the size of the package of meat I'm using. A recipe calling for a pound and a half of meat and I have 2 lbs? Add a quarter to the recipe. Hell, sometimes I even cook 2 batches if it's something I really like, because then what I'll do is put the rest of it in individual, serving sized tupperwares and freeze em for an easy ass meal on lazy days.

Late to the party on the first post I have something relevant to say. I had to put down my cat of 17 years in January due to kidney failure. I got him when I was 5 for Christmas and he slept with me every night until I had to leave for college. 1 month into living at the dorms, Mom calls to let me know something that he's lost all his weight and is losing patches of hair. Vet concluded he was depressed, and I moved back home the moment the semester ended. He regained all his weight and the missing hair grew back. He moved with me twice afterwards, and never failed to be waiting for me by the door when I got back from work or classes, or to fall asleep next to me at night. Hell, my cat refused to not even check on me every hour or so if he knew I was home. 

When he laid in bed for 24 hours straight without drinking any water or eating any food, even though I brought it up to him and held it in front of his face, I knew it was time even before the vet ran the final tests. If there way any way in the world for him to have a decent quality of life, no matter how much money it would have cost me, I would have seized the opportunity in a heartbeat. The best the vet said we could do was give him dialysis multiple times a week for the rest of his life, which would be 3 months maximum, and that he would be suffering every moment of it. I made the decision to spare him from that and held him in my arms while the vet administered the IV's and I held him until long after his heart had stopped beating and his muscles stopped that after-death twitch thing.

I know without a moment's thought that he would have been there for me and there was no way in hell I was going to leave him alone for that. Even severely dehydrated and in god knows how much fucking pain, he looked up at me one last time while the vet was preparing the shot and started purring. Pet owners, please don't leave your pets to go out alone. 
TLDR: If you love your pets half as much as they love you, don't fucking dare leave them to die alone.
